analogy.p: Asexual reproduction is like a **photocopier**: every copy of the page is identical, quick and cheap, and if the page has a mistake every copy has it. Sexual reproduction is like **shuffling two decks of recipe cards** and dealing a new hand to each child: every hand is different, so if a new problem appears (a food allergy) some hands will still work. It takes longer and needs two decks. The analogy breaks down because real offspring get exactly half their genes from each parent and gene combinations are made by chance in meiosis, not dealt deliberately.

bullets: **Sexual reproduction** = the **fusion of male and female gametes** (fertilisation). It needs **two parents** and the offspring contain a **mixture of their parents' genes**.
**Asexual reproduction** = only **one parent**, **no fusion of gametes**, so the offspring are **genetically identical** to the parent (they are **clones**).
**Meiosis** is the cell division that produces **gametes**; **mitosis** is the cell division involved in asexual reproduction and growth.
Know the **sites of gamete production**: testes and ovaries in animals; anthers and ovaries in flowering plants.
Triple (Biology only) content: **advantages and disadvantages** of sexual and asexual reproduction, and examples of organisms that use both.
Command words: **describe** (say what happens), **explain** (give reasons, use 'because'), **compare** (similarities AND differences), **evaluate** (weigh up both sides and reach a judgement).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8461 section 4.6.1 (Reproduction) asks you to know the difference between **sexual** and **asexual reproduction**, to describe **meiosis** as the type of cell division that makes **gametes**, and (Biology only) to evaluate the **advantages and disadvantages** of each. You also need examples of organisms that use both methods: **malarial parasites**, **fungi** and **plants**. This matters because nearly every later idea in inheritance, variation, evolution and selective breeding depends on whether offspring are identical to their parent or genetically different.

bullets: **Gamete** = a sex cell. Male gametes: **sperm** (animals) and **pollen nuclei** (plants). Female gametes: **egg cells / ova** (animals) and **egg cells in the ovule** (plants).
**Fertilisation** = fusion of the nucleus of a male gamete with the nucleus of a female gamete.
The **zygote** (fertilised egg) is **diploid**, containing a full set of chromosomes: **23 from the mother and 23 from the father** in humans, making 46.
Gametes are **haploid** (one set of chromosomes: 23 in humans). If they were diploid, chromosome number would **double every generation**.
The zygote divides by **mitosis**, so every body cell of the offspring carries the same DNA as the zygote.
The mixing of genes from two parents is the source of **variation** between individuals of the same species.
Examples: humans, other mammals, birds, most flowering plants (seeds), most insects.
core.p: In sexual reproduction a **male gamete** and a **female gamete** join in **fertilisation** to form a single cell called a **zygote**. The zygote then divides by **mitosis** many times and the cells **differentiate** to form an embryo and eventually an adult. Because the genetic information in the offspring comes from **two different parents**, and because each gamete is itself genetically different from every other gamete, the offspring are **not identical** to either parent or to their brothers and sisters (except identical twins).

bullets: In **animals**, meiosis happens in the **testes** (making sperm) and **ovaries** (making eggs).
In **flowering plants**, meiosis happens in the **anthers** (making pollen grains containing male gametes) and in the **ovules inside the ovary** (making the female gamete).
Body cells in humans have **23 pairs of chromosomes (46)**; gametes have **23 single chromosomes**.
Meiosis involves **one DNA copy and two divisions**, producing **four haploid, genetically different** cells.
**Fertilisation restores the diploid number**: 23 + 23 = 46.
Mitosis (for comparison) makes **two genetically identical diploid** cells.
core.p: Gametes are made by **meiosis** in the **reproductive organs**. A body cell with the full diploid number of chromosomes first **copies its genetic information** (DNA replication), then **divides twice**, giving **four cells**, each with only **one set of chromosomes**. Every one of those four gametes is **genetically different** from the others. The full step-by-step process is in the Meiosis note; here the key point is *why* it exists: halving the chromosome number means fertilisation can restore the correct number.

bullets: Only **one parent** is needed; no mate has to be found.
**Mitosis** is the cell division used; no meiosis and no gametes are involved.
Offspring are **genetically identical** to the parent and to each other: **no genetic variation** (apart from rare mutations).
It is **faster** and uses **less time and energy** than sexual reproduction (no need to grow flowers, make gametes or find a mate).
Many identical offspring can be made **quickly in favourable conditions**, so a population can grow very fast.
Examples: bacteria (binary fission), some plants (runners, bulbs, tubers), some fungi (spores), **Hydra** budding, and cloning (e.g. cuttings, tissue culture).
core.p: In **asexual reproduction** a **single parent** produces offspring **without gametes fusing**. The cells of the parent divide by **mitosis**, so the offspring receive an **exact copy** of the parent's genes. They are therefore **genetically identical clones**. Any differences between asexually produced offspring are caused by the **environment** (for example one plantlet getting more light), not by genes. Asexual reproduction is quick and needs no mate, which makes it a very successful strategy for organisms that live in stable, favourable conditions.

bullets: **Parents**: two (sexual) vs one (asexual).
**Gametes**: made by meiosis and fuse (sexual) vs none and no fusion (asexual).
**Cell division**: meiosis (to make gametes) then mitosis (to grow) vs mitosis only.
**Offspring**: genetically different from each other and the parents vs genetically identical.
**Variation**: lots vs none.
**Speed and energy**: slower, more energy needed vs faster, less energy needed.
**Similarity**: in both, offspring grow by **mitosis** and both pass genetic information to the next generation.
core.p: Examiners often ask you to **compare** the two methods, which means giving similarities **and** differences. The most important difference is the genetic one: sexual reproduction creates **variation**, asexual reproduction creates **clones**. Everything else (number of parents, gametes, type of cell division, speed) follows from that. Always write comparisons in a form like 'In sexual reproduction ... whereas in asexual reproduction ...' so the mark scheme can see both sides.

bullets: It produces **variation in the offspring**.
If the environment changes, **variation gives a survival advantage** because some individuals will be better adapted.
This increases the chance that **the species survives** (not that every individual survives).
Humans can use the variation in **selective breeding** to produce animals and crops with desirable characteristics (e.g. high milk yield, disease resistance).
Linked idea: variation is the raw material of **evolution by natural selection**.
Exam phrase: 'variation means some individuals may be resistant / better adapted, so they survive and reproduce, passing on their alleles'.
core.p: The big advantage of sexual reproduction is **variation**. Because offspring differ genetically, a population contains many different **alleles** and combinations. If the environment changes (new disease, climate change, new predator) there is a better chance that **at least some individuals have characteristics that let them survive and reproduce**. Those survivors pass on their alleles, which is **natural selection**. This is why sexual reproduction helps a **species survive in a changing environment**.

bullets: **Two parents** are needed, so a mate must be found (difficult for isolated or rare organisms).
It **takes more time and energy** than asexual reproduction (growing flowers, producing gametes, finding a mate, pregnancy).
Offspring are produced **more slowly**, so the population grows more slowly.
Genes from **both** parents are mixed, so a **well-adapted combination in one parent is not copied exactly**.
In plants it relies on pollination (wind, insects) which may not happen.
Only half of each parent's genes are passed to each offspring.
core.p: Sexual reproduction has costs. It needs **two parents**, so an organism must **find a mate**, and in plants it needs pollination and often a pollinator. It **takes more time and energy** because gametes, flowers, courtship and sometimes parental care are required. Offspring are produced more slowly and in smaller numbers than by cloning. And, importantly, there is **no guarantee** a successful combination of genes will be passed on, because the genes are shuffled each generation.

bullets: **Only one parent** is needed.
It is **more time-efficient and energy-efficient** (no need to find a mate or make gametes).
**Many identical offspring** can be produced **faster**.
Good for **quickly colonising** a favourable habitat.
Offspring keep the **successful characteristics** of the parent (useful for crops, e.g. strawberries and bananas).
Linked idea: **cloning** and **tissue culture** exploit asexual reproduction to produce identical plants for growers.
core.p: Asexual reproduction is best when **conditions are stable and favourable**. Because the offspring are **identical clones of a successful parent**, they are already well adapted to that environment, so a farmer or a bacterium can quickly produce many individuals that will all do well. It is also very **efficient**: only one parent is needed, no energy is spent on gametes or finding a mate, and many offspring can be made in a short time.

bullets: **No genetic variation** in the population (clones).
A **single disease or environmental change** could wipe out the whole population.
Harmful alleles are copied to **every** offspring.
Example: a crop grown as clones (e.g. bananas) is very vulnerable to one new fungal disease.
The species cannot **evolve** quickly through natural selection without variation (only mutations add new alleles).
Exam phrase: 'all offspring are genetically identical so if conditions change, none may be adapted, so all could die'.
core.p: The main weakness of asexual reproduction is the **lack of genetic variation**. Because every individual in the population is genetically identical, they all share the **same weaknesses**. If the environment changes or a new disease arrives, **all** of them may be killed, because none has a different, resistant allele. Asexual reproduction therefore helps a population in a **stable** environment but is risky in a **changing** one.

bullets: Asexual stage: **in the human host** (fast multiplication).
Sexual stage: **in the mosquito** (variation, including possible drug resistance).
Variation produced helps the parasite **survive** attempts to treat it (e.g. drug-resistant strains arise).
The mosquito is the **vector**: it carries the parasite from person to person.
Controlling the mosquito (nets, repellent, draining water) breaks the life cycle.
Compare: the same species uses asexual reproduction when conditions are good and sexual when variation is useful.
core.h: Organisms that use both methods: malarial parasites
core.p: The **malarial parasite** (*Plasmodium*) reproduces **both ways** during its life cycle. Inside the **human host** it reproduces **asexually**, multiplying quickly in liver and red blood cells, which causes the disease. Inside the **mosquito** it reproduces **sexually**, which creates variation. This lets the parasite exploit a favourable host rapidly while still producing new genetic combinations.

bullets: **Fungi**: spores (asexual, clones) and sexual reproduction (variation).
**Strawberry plants**: **runners** are stems that grow sideways and form new plantlets (asexual, identical).
**Daffodils**: **bulbs** divide to form new bulbs (asexual).
Potatoes grow new plants from **tubers** (asexual).
Flowering plants also make **seeds** by sexual reproduction (variation and dispersal).
Asexual spread is quick and keeps good traits; sexual reproduction gives variation for survival in change.
core.h: Organisms that use both methods: fungi and plants
core.p: Many **fungi** reproduce **asexually by producing spores** (mitosis), which spread easily and grow into new fungi that are clones, but they can also reproduce **sexually** to give variation. Many **plants** reproduce sexually using seeds from flowers, and asexually using **runners** (strawberry), **bulbs** (daffodil) or tubers (potato). Switching between methods lets the organism use the best strategy for its conditions.

bullets: Humans: **testes** make **sperm**; **ovaries** make **egg cells (ova)**.
Plants: **anther** makes **pollen**; **ovary (ovules)** contains the **egg cell**.
Gamete production takes place by **meiosis** in these organs.
Reproductive organs also make hormones (testosterone, oestrogen, progesterone).
Gametes are specialised: sperm have a tail and many mitochondria, eggs are large with food store.
Fertilisation joins the nuclei, giving a zygote with the diploid number.
core.p: You must be able to name where gametes are made in animals and plants. In **humans**, the male gametes (sperm) are made in the **testes** and the female gametes (egg cells) in the **ovaries**. In **flowering plants**, the male gametes are in **pollen grains** made in the **anthers**, and the female gametes are in the **ovules** inside the **ovary**. All of these are sites of **meiosis**.

bullets: Body (somatic) cell: **46** (23 pairs), diploid.
Gamete: **23**, haploid.
Zygote: **46**, diploid (23 + 23).
After mitosis: each daughter cell has **46**.
After meiosis: each daughter cell has **23**.
If a species has diploid number 2n = 14, its gametes have 7 and its zygote has 14.
One pair of the 23 is the **sex chromosomes** (XX female, XY male); the others are autosomes.
core.p: **Diploid** means two sets of chromosomes; **haploid** means one set. Human body cells are diploid with **46 chromosomes in 23 pairs**, one of each pair from each parent. Gametes are haploid with **23 chromosomes**. Keeping track of these numbers is a very common exam question, and the logic is always the same: meiosis halves the number, fertilisation restores it, mitosis keeps it constant.

bullets: **Meiosis** note: step-by-step gamete formation.
**DNA and the genome**: genes are on chromosomes in the nucleus.
**Genetic inheritance**: alleles in gametes combine at fertilisation.
**Natural selection / selective breeding**: need variation, mainly from sexual reproduction.
**Cloning (triple)**: cuttings, tissue culture, embryo transplants and adult cell cloning.
**Resistant bacteria**: bacteria reproduce asexually, so a resistant mutant produces resistant clones.
core.p: This topic is the entrance to the whole of Unit 4.6. **Variation** from sexual reproduction is what **natural selection** acts on; **cloning** and **tissue culture** use asexual reproduction; **genetic engineering** is a way to add new alleles; **inherited disorders** and **Punnett squares** follow from alleles in gametes; and **evolution** and **antibiotic resistance** in bacteria depend on mutation and selection in populations that may reproduce asexually.

exam: **1 mark** definitions: give the key phrase, e.g. 'fusion of male and female gametes' (sexual) or 'one parent, genetically identical offspring' (asexual).
**Compare** (2 to 4 marks): use 'whereas' and give a difference for both methods; a one-sided statement scores less.
**Explain** why variation helps: variation, so some individuals are adapted/resistant, so they survive and reproduce, passing on alleles.
**Evaluate** (6 marks): give advantages and disadvantages of both, link to the scenario (stable vs changing environment), then a clear judgement.
Always say **'genetically identical'**, not 'the same' or 'similar'.
Link asexual disadvantage to **'all vulnerable to the same disease'** and sexual disadvantage to **'needs two parents, slower'**.
Chromosome number questions: meiosis **halves** (n), fertilisation **restores** (2n), mitosis **keeps** 2n.
Name organs precisely: **testes, ovaries, anthers, ovules/ovary**.
For malaria, state which stage is in which organism (asexual in human, sexual in mosquito).
Data questions: if offspring show no differences in a trait, suggest asexual reproduction; large differences suggest sexual.

mistakes.w: Asexual offspring are 'similar' to the parent.

mistakes.r: Variation gives an advantage **in a changing environment**; in a stable one, asexual can be better.
mistakes.w: Sexual reproduction always gives a survival advantage.

mistakes.r: Without variation, a **change** such as a new disease may kill **all** of them; say why.
It needs **less** time and energy than sexual reproduction.
Fertilisation is when gametes **fuse**; meiosis makes them.
**Asexually in the human host**, **sexually in the mosquito**.
mistakes.w: Malaria parasites reproduce sexually in humans.

summary: The spec asks you to describe sexual reproduction (fusion of gametes, two parents, genetic variation) and asexual reproduction (one parent, mitosis, clones), to link gamete formation to meiosis, and (Biology only) to evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of each, with examples such as malaria parasites, fungi and plants. It matters because whether offspring are identical or different underlies inheritance, evolution and selective breeding.

terms.d: Reproduction involving the fusion of male and female gametes; two parents; offspring have a mixture of their parents' genes.
Reproduction involving only one parent and no fusion of gametes; offspring are genetically identical to the parent (clones).
A sex cell (sperm, egg cell, pollen nucleus); haploid.
The fusion of the nucleus of a male gamete with the nucleus of a female gamete.
The cell formed when two gametes fuse; the first cell of a new individual; diploid.
A type of cell division in the reproductive organs that produces genetically different gametes with half the number of chromosomes.
Cell division producing two genetically identical diploid cells; used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.
A cell with a single set of chromosomes (23 in humans).
A cell with two sets of chromosomes (46 in humans).
An organism genetically identical to its parent.
Differences between individuals of the same species.
A horizontal stem that grows from a plant and forms new plantlets by asexual reproduction (e.g. strawberry).
An underground storage organ from which new plants grow by asexual reproduction (e.g. daffodil).
The part of the stamen in a flower that produces pollen containing the male gametes.
In animals, the organ that makes egg cells; in plants, the structure containing the ovules.
The male organ that makes sperm.

worked.ans: Sexual reproduction needs two parents and the fusion of male and female gametes, so the offspring are genetically different from the parents and each other, whereas asexual reproduction needs only one parent and no gametes, so the offspring are genetically identical clones. Asexual reproduction is also faster and uses less energy than sexual reproduction, which needs a mate to be found.
worked.q: Compare sexual and asexual reproduction. (4 marks)
steps: Parents: sexual has two, asexual has one.
Gametes: sexual involves fusion of gametes; asexual does not.
Offspring: sexual offspring are genetically different (variation); asexual offspring are clones.
Speed/energy: asexual is faster and uses less energy.

worked.ans: The plants are clones with identical genes, so there is no variation. None has a resistant allele, so all are equally susceptible to the fungus and the whole crop could be destroyed.
worked.q: A farm grows bananas as clones. A new fungal disease appears. Explain why the whole crop may be destroyed. (3 marks)
steps: Bananas are grown by asexual reproduction, so the plants are genetically identical.
So they all have the same susceptibility; no resistant alleles.
If the fungus can infect one plant it can infect all.
